requirements.lead_text: Handling a First Aid Emergency. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Handling a First Aid Emergency. Do the following: (a) Explain the steps necessary to assess and handle a first aid emergency, including a safety evaluation of the scene. (b) Tell how you would obtain emergency medical assistance from your home and from a remote location on a wilderness camping trip. (c) Demonstrate the precautions you must take to reduce the risk of transmitting an infection between you and the victim while administering first aid, including the safe disposal of used first aid supplies. (d) Demonstrate evaluation of and management of a patient's airway and breathing. (e) Demonstrate a thorough examination of an accident victim. (f) Discuss why shock is an emergency. (g) Define the term triage and describe examples of triage situations that you may encounter.

Handling a First Aid Emergency Principle 2: To do this, get the help of others in your group and lift the victim in the same position as found (p. 19).
Handling a First Aid Emergency Principle 3: Remember: Do not move the victim unless you absolutely have to for safety reasons (p. 19).
Handling a First Aid Emergency Principle 4: It is impossible to know for sure if the victim has any diseases (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Handling a First Aid Emergency): You should consider all body fluids to be infectious (p. 19).
Step 2 (Handling a First Aid Emergency): Wear nonlatex gloves and, if you might be splashed by blood, vomit, or other body fluids, also wear a protective mask and eye shield (p. 19).
Step 3 (Handling a First Aid Emergency): Your sunglasses, rain gear, and bandana or neckerchief (over your mouth and nose) would work if nothing else is available (p. 19).
Step 4 (Handling a First Aid Emergency): Provide Urgent Treatment If the person is Breathing and bleeding, these are your immediate concerns when treating the victim of an accident (p. 19).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a woodland trail hike, your patrol discovers an adult hiker lying at the base of a wet rock ledge with bright red blood spurting from a lower-leg wound and a downed power line 25 feet uphill. What is your patrol's immediate first-aid sequence?
quiz_item.question: During a woodland trail hike, your patrol discovers an adult hiker lying at the base of a wet rock ledge with bright red blood spurting from a lower-leg wound and a downed power line 25 feet uphill. What is your patrol's immediate first-aid sequence?
options: A. Sprint straight to the victim without gloves to apply a tourniquet before checking the overhead wire.

B. Stop and size up scene safety first (confirm the downed wire does not endanger the approach zone), put on nitrile gloves for Universal Precautions, direct a buddy to call 911 with GPS coordinates, and apply firm direct pressure with a sterile gauze dressing to control arterial bleeding.
C. Have two Scouts carry the hiker 100 yards down the rocky trail before checking airway, breathing, or severe bleeding.
D. Pour cold stream water onto the open arterial wound and elevate both legs 18 inches before checking scene hazards.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Stop and size up scene safety first (confirm the downed wire does not endanger the approach zone), put on nitrile gloves for Universal Precautions, direct a buddy to call 911 with GPS coordinates, and apply firm direct pressure with a sterile gauze dressing to control arterial bleeding.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Under the First Aid Merit Badge Pamphlet emergency action sequence (Check-Call-Care), rescuers must first verify scene safety so they do not become a second victim, apply Universal Precautions (BSI barriers), summon EMS immediately, and treat life-threatening conditions (airway, breathing, severe bleeding) before minor injuries.

requirements.lead_text: Preparing for First Aid Emergencies. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Preparing for First Aid Emergencies. Do the following: (a) Obtain a copy of the Scout Annual Health and Medical Record and discuss the importance of the form including information on immunizations, allergies, medications, health history, and medical examinations to providing first aid at Scouting events. (b) Using checklists provided in the First Aid merit badge pamphlet or ones approved by your counselor, do the following: (1) Assemble a personal first-aid kit for hiking and backpacking. Demonstrate the proper use of each item in your first-aid kit to your counselor. (2) With your counselor, inspect a unit, home, vehicle, or camp first-aid kit and discuss your findings.

Preparing for First Aid Emergencies Principle 2: Having it back at camp does no good when it is needed on the trail (p. 93).

Preparing for First Aid Emergencies Principle 4: Step 2, Check the victim for a medical ID bracelet, necklace, or information card (p. 93).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Preparing for First Aid Emergencies): Ask if the person is carrying a prescribed emergency medical kit (p. 93).
Step 2 (Preparing for First Aid Emergencies): You might be able to assist the person under certain circumstances AND if you are trained and allowed to assist by state or local regulations (p. 93).
Step 3 (Preparing for First Aid Emergencies): If so, follow the kit instructions exactly and assist the person by locating the medication kit and handing it to him (p. 93).
Step 4 (Preparing for First Aid Emergencies): It is best that the individual administers the medication (p. 93).

requirements.lead_text: Wounds with No External Bleeding. Describe the symptoms and signs of, show first aid for, and explain prevention of these wounds:
requirements.req_text: Wounds with No External Bleeding. Describe the symptoms and signs of, show first aid for, and explain prevention of these wounds: (a) Closed wounds, such as a bruise (contusion) or a hematoma (b) Superficial, partial thickness, and full thickness thermal (heat) burns or scalds (c) Chemical burns (d) Electrical burns (e) Sunburn (f) Snow blindness (g) Immersion foot, frostnip, frostbite, and ice burns (h) Abrasions, such as chafing and rope burns (i) Blisters on the hands, feet, buttocks, and shoulders (j) Puncture wounds from splinters, rope splinters, nails, and fish hooks (k) Rash from poisonous plants (l) Bug bites of chiggers, ticks, mosquitoes, and biting gnats (m) Bee stings (n) Bites of spiders (o) Sting of a scorpion (p) Bite of a pet or wild mammal or human (q) Bite of a venomous snake

pamphlet_excerpts: Wounds with No External Bleeding: The bites of mosquitoes, chiggers, and nosee-ums are irritating but not usually dangerous (p. 14).
Wounds with No External Bleeding Principle 2: More troublesome are ticks, some spiders, and some ants (p. 14).
Wounds with No External Bleeding Principle 3: To avoid getting bitten by ticks, wear long pants and along-sleeved shirt whenever you are in tick infested woodlands and fields (p. 14).
Wounds with No External Bleeding Principle 4: Button your collar and tuck your pant cuffs into your boots or socks (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Inspect yourself daily, especially the hairy parts of your body, and immediately remove any ticks you find (p. 14).
Step 2 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Ticks bury their heads beneath the skin of their victims (p. 14).
Step 3 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): To remove a tick, with gloved hands, grasp it with tweezers close to the skin and gently pull until it comes loose (p. 14).
Step 4 (Wounds with No External Bleeding): Don't squeeze, twist, or jerk the tick, as doing so could leave its mouth parts still buried in the skin (p. 14).

Patrol trauma and first-aid kit (sterile gauze, roller bandages, triangular cravats, SAM splint)
Non-latex nitrile exam gloves, CPR breathing barrier mask, and antiseptic swabs.
Emergency action plan checklist and simulated patient assessment cards.

pamphlet_excerpts: Bleeding Wounds: Cuts and Scrapes (Abrasions) Cuts may be caused by knives, razors, or broken glass (p. 37).
Bleeding Wounds Principle 2: An abrasion is a wound that occurs as a result of the outer layers of the skin being rubbed or scraped (p. 37).
Bleeding Wounds Principle 3: Abrasions may happen when the skin is scraped against a hard surface, for example, when a bicyclist falls onto the pavement (p. 37).
Bleeding Wounds Principle 4: Sometimes dirt and gravel get ground into the abrasion, which increases the likelihood of infection (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Bleeding Wounds): To protect yourself from cuts and scrapes, dress appropriately for the activity, for instance, jeans, boots, gloves, longsleeved shirt (p. 37).
Step 2 (Bleeding Wounds): A few simple precautions can help you avoid the pain of the treatment and healing process (p. 37).
Step 3 (Bleeding Wounds): Treat a minor cut or scrape by flushing the area with clean water for at least five minutes, or until all foreign matter appears to be washed away (p. 37).
Step 4 (Bleeding Wounds): Remember to protect yourself withnonlatex gloves and other precautions as needed, as well asby washing your hands before and after treating (p. 37).

pamphlet_excerpts: Breathing Emergencies: If you suspect that frostbite extends below skin level, removewet clothing and wrap the injured area in a dry blanket (p. 61).
Breathing Emergencies Principle 2: Get the victim under the care of a physician as soon as possible (p. 61).
Breathing Emergencies Principle 3: Rewarm the area only if there is no chance of refreezing (p. 61).
Breathing Emergencies Principle 4: To treat frostnip, move the victim into a tent or building, then warm the injured area (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Breathing Emergencies): If an ear or cheek is frozen, remove a glove and warm the injury with the palm of your hand (p. 61).
Step 2 (Breathing Emergencies): Slip a frost nipped hand under your clothing and tuck it beneath an armpit (p. 61).
Step 3 (Breathing Emergencies): Treat frost nipped toes by putting the victim's bare feet against the warm skin of your belly (p. 61).
Step 4 (Breathing Emergencies): The human body is 70 percent water, which is essential to maintain our body temperature (p. 61).

pamphlet_excerpts: Loss of Consciousness: Taking too many drugs or drinking too much alcohol can make aperson lose consciousness (p. 63).
Loss of Consciousness Principle 2: Never give an unconscious person anything to drink, throw water on the face, or offer stimulants such as smelling salts (p. 63).
Loss of Consciousness Principle 3: Do not shake or slap the person in an effort to wake him orher (p. 63).
Loss of Consciousness Principle 4: A loss of consciousness for more than two minutes is a serious medical condition (p. 63).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Loss of Consciousness): An unconscious person might have been hit in the head or had a heart attack or stroke (p. 63).
Step 2 (Loss of Consciousness): People with diabetes can lose consciousness from either very high or very low blood sugar (p. 63).
Step 3 (Loss of Consciousness): Look for an emergency medical ID bracelet or necklace or an information card that identifies health problems such as diabetes (p. 63).
Step 4 (Loss of Consciousness): Whenever a person is unconscious for more than a minute or two, call 911 or your local emergency-response number for medical assistance (p. 63).

pamphlet_excerpts: Heart Attack: Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries The human body works best if it has a constant temperature (p. 59).
Heart Attack Principle 2: A person who is exposed to cold environmental conditions and loses body heat faster than it can be generated will be in grave danger (p. 59).
Heart Attack Principle 3: The person's body temperature may become too low to support life (p. 59).
Heart Attack Principle 4: Likewise, a person whose body has overheated and cannot cool itself sufficiently may die if fast emergency medical care cannot be found (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Heart Attack): These temperature related emergencies require fast, lifesaving first aid (p. 59).
Step 2 (Heart Attack): Hypothermia occurs when a person's body is losing more heat than it can generate (p. 59).
Step 3 (Heart Attack): It is a danger for anyone who is not dressed warmly enough, although exposure to cold is seldom the only cause (p. 59).
Step 4 (Heart Attack): Dehydration is a common contributing factor to hypothermia (p. 59).

requirements.req_text: Muscle and Bone Injuries. Do the following: (a) Explain the similarities and differences in a strain, a muscle tear, a tendon rupture, a sprain, a dislocation, a simple fracture, and a compound fracture. (b) Describe the symptoms and signs of and first aid for a muscle strain, a muscle tear, and a tendon rupture. (c) Describe the symptoms and signs of, and potential complications of, a sprain, a fracture, and a dislocation. (d) Demonstrate bandages for these injuries: (1) Arm slings for forearm or upper arm or collarbone fractures (2) Elastic wrap and cravat bandages for ankle sprain (3) Elastic wrap and cravat bandages for wrist sprain or hand injury (e) Demonstrate the proper procedures for handling and splinting of suspected closed or open fractures or dislocations of the: (1) Finger and toe (2) Forearm or wrist (3) Upper leg (4) Lower leg or ankle

Muscle and Bone Injuries Principle 3: Most of the time a victim will have just one injury that isnot life threatening (p. 45).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Muscle and Bone Injuries): Begin treatment only after determining the number and location of the injuries (p. 45).
Step 2 (Muscle and Bone Injuries): A "yes" answer suggests that the person might have a fracture (p. 45).
Step 3 (Muscle and Bone Injuries): Many people believe if they can move the part, the bone isnot broken (p. 45).
Step 4 (Muscle and Bone Injuries): Although they might be reluctant to doso, many people can voluntarily move a fractured part (p. 45).

pamphlet_excerpts: Head and Spine Injuries: Place the forearm in a sling with the hand raised higher than the elbow, then tie the upperarm against the side of the body with awide cravat bandage (p. 41).
Head and Spine Injuries Principle 2: Placing the splinted arm in a sling with the hand slightly raised will also immobilize the elbow joint (p. 41).
Head and Spine Injuries Principle 3: The backbone (spinal column) is made up of small bones called vertebrae that surround and protect the spinal cord (p. 41).
Head and Spine Injuries Principle 4: If avertebra is broken or dislocated, the spinal cord may be injured (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Head and Spine Injuries): Fractures of the neck and back are extremely dangerous, because movement might further damage the spinal cord and cause permanent paralysis or even (p. 41).
Step 2 (Head and Spine Injuries): Whenever someone has fallen, been involved in an automobile accident, or suffered a blow to the head, assume there is an injury to the neck (p. 41).
Step 3 (Head and Spine Injuries): The victim may or may not be suffering from pain, paralysis, cuts and bruises, or swelling (p. 41).
Step 4 (Head and Spine Injuries): The injured area may be deformed or abnormally shaped, or there maybe no symptoms at all (p. 41).

pamphlet_excerpts: Moving a Patient: When a person must be moved for some distance or his or her injuries are serious, you should carry the person on a stretcher (p. 15).
Moving a Patient Principle 2: When available, use a litter or rescue basket made especially for transporting injured persons (p. 15).
Moving a Patient Principle 3: Make a stretcherout of two poles (longer than the victim is tall), for example, strong branches, tool handles, oars, orthe poles from a wall tent (p. 15).
Moving a Patient Principle 4: Secure two Scout shirts (insideout, with all the buttons buttoned) over the poles to form astretcher (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Moving a Patient): If possible, overlap the bottoms of the shirts to form a more secure bedding (p. 15).
Step 2 (Moving a Patient): Explain the steps (procedures) in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) (p. 15).
Step 3 (Moving a Patient): One way to stay healthy and safe both at home and when you are in the out-of-doors is to recognize that there is an element of risk in many activities (p. 15).
Step 4 (Moving a Patient): By being aware of risk and adjusting your behavior to manage it, you will also bein a stronger position to provide assistance (p. 15).

Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions Principle 4: One type of heatstroke develops in young, healthy people from dehydration and over exertion in hot weather, especially in high humidity (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions): The first sign of true heat stroke is often collapse (p. 59).
Step 2 (Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions): On a hot day, if someone collapses without warning, you must consider heatstroke (p. 59).
Step 3 (Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions): The other type of heatstroke usually happens in elderly people when the weather is very hot, especially with high humidity (p. 59).
Step 4 (Heat- and Cold-Related Conditions): The signals are similar to exercise-related heatstroke except that the skin is hot and dry because there is no sweating (p. 59).

pamphlet_excerpts: Mental Health Conditions: How to Handle an Emergency How to Handle an Emergency Even the best plans can fall apart (p. 17).
Mental Health Conditions Principle 2: Most of the time first aid is relatively simple because you are dealing with a single injury or illness (p. 17).
Mental Health Conditions Principle 3: You must, however, be prepared to handle more complex situations (p. 17).
Mental Health Conditions Principle 4: You might be the first to arrive or the most qualified, thus the person who is most able to take charge (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Mental Health Conditions): Good Samaritan laws protect anyone making a good-faith effort to help the victim of an injury or illness (p. 17).
Step 2 (Mental Health Conditions): Whenever you are confronted with a first-aidemergency, use your skills to the best of your ability and training (p. 17).
Step 3 (Mental Health Conditions): No one expects you to have the knowledge of a physician (p. 17).
Step 4 (Mental Health Conditions): However, Scouting's history is filled with stories of Scouts who used their training to help others, sometimes even saving lives. 1 (p. 17).

pamphlet_excerpts: Miscellaneous Conditions: Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries Heatstroke Heatstroke, much more serious than heat exhaustion, can lead to death if not treated immediately (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 2: Left untreated, heat exhaustion can develop into heatstroke (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 3: In heatstroke, the body's cooling system begins to fail and the person's core temperature rises to life-threatening levels (above 105 degrees) (p. 63).
Miscellaneous Conditions Principle 4: One type of heatstroke develops in young, healthy people from dehydration and over exertion in hot weather, especially in high humidity (p. 63).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The first sign of true heat stroke is often collapse (p. 63).
Step 2 (Miscellaneous Conditions): On a hot day, if someone collapses without warning, you must consider heatstroke (p. 63).
Step 3 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The other type of heatstroke usually happens in elderly people when the weather is very hot, especially with high humidity (p. 63).
Step 4 (Miscellaneous Conditions): The signals are similar to exercise-related heatstroke except that the skin is hot and dry because there is no sweating (p. 63).

pamphlet_excerpts: Teach a first-aid skill or topic: Moving an Ill or Injured Person The decision to move an accident victim should be made carefully (p. 29).

Teach a first-aid skill or topic Principle 2: In many cases, there will be emergency medical crews, fire department personnel, or others with special equipment and training who will transport (p. 29).

Teach a first-aid skill or topic Principle 3: If, however, someone is in danger from fire, smoke, water, electrical hazards, poisonous gases, exposure, or other immediate danger, you must move (p. 29).
Teach a first-aid skill or topic Principle 4: You might also need to move an injured person in order to give that person proper care, or reach another victim (p. 29).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Teach a first-aid skill or topic): Move the person only as far as is necessary, and do not endanger yourself (p. 29).
Step 2 (Teach a first-aid skill or topic): Sometimes you will find that a victim's injuries are minor enough that the person can move with some assistance (p. 29).
Step 3 (Teach a first-aid skill or topic): Before attempting to move someone, make sure the person is not suffering from any of the following conditions (p. 29).
Step 4 (Teach a first-aid skill or topic): When time is critical, you might need to decide between moving the person to a place where they can get care or waiting for help to come (p. 29).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit an emergency medical station house or training center in person. From the medical first responders that you meet during your visit, learn about how they serve their community and about their careers. Discuss with your counselor what you learned during your tour and interviews. (b) Interview an emergency medical services professional about their work. Learn about how they chose this career and about their duties. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (c) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in emergency medical services. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities, and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (d) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in the field of emergency medical services to pursue a personal hobby and/or healthy lifestyle. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

pamphlet_excerpts: First Aid Careers and Pathways: Visit an emergency medical station house: Moving an Ill or Injured Person The decision to move an accident victim should be made carefully (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 2: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 2: In many cases, there will be emergency medical crews, fire department personnel, or others with special equipment and training who will transport (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 3: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 3: If, however, someone is in danger from fire, smoke, water, electrical hazards, poisonous gases, exposure, or other immediate danger, you must move (p. 25).

First Aid Careers and Pathways Principle 4: Visit an emergency medical station house Principle 4: You might also need to move an injured person in order to give that person proper care, or reach another victim (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 1 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Move the person only as far as is necessary, and do not endanger yourself (p. 25).

Step 2 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 2 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Sometimes you will find that a victim's injuries are minor enough that the person can move with some assistance (p. 25).

Step 3 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 3 (Visit an emergency medical station house): Before attempting to move someone, make sure the person is not suffering from any of the following conditions (p. 25).

Step 4 (First Aid Careers and Pathways): Step 4 (Visit an emergency medical station house): When time is critical, you might need to decide between moving the person to a place where they can get care or waiting for help to come (p. 25).

D. Pour cold stream water onto the open arterial wound and elevate both legs 18 inches before checking scene hazards.
